questions.prompt: What is the primary difference between session-based authentication and token-based (JWT) authentication?

options.text: JWTs are stored exclusively in server memory, whereas sessions are stored in the browser.
Sessions require server-side state storage, whereas JWTs are self-contained and stateless.
Sessions are immune to XSS attacks, while JWTs are immune to CSRF attacks.
JWTs require a database lookup on every single request, while sessions do not.

questions.explanation: Session-based authentication typically relies on server-side storage (like a database or memory cache) to validate the session ID, whereas JWTs contain all necessary user and claims data signed cryptographically, making them stateless.

questions.prompt: When designing a secure token-based authentication system using JSON Web Tokens (JWT), which of the following practices should be followed regarding the secret key or private key?

options.text: Embed the private key in the frontend JavaScript bundle so the client can sign requests.
Store the secret key securely on the server and never expose it to the client.
Rotate the secret key on every incoming HTTP request to prevent replay attacks.
Use an easily guessable secret key to ensure fast hashing performance.

questions.explanation: The secret or private key used to sign JWTs must remain strictly on the server to prevent malicious clients from forging valid tokens with arbitrary claims.

questions.prompt: In an OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow, why is the Authorization Code exchanged for an Access Token on the backend server rather than directly in the client browser?

options.text: Browsers do not support HTTP POST requests required for token exchange.
It keeps the client secret hidden from public view and potential theft.
Backend servers execute token exchanges significantly faster than client browsers.
Authorization codes expire instantly once they reach a browser environment.

questions.explanation: The backend server can securely store credentials like the client secret without exposing them to public-facing environments like single-page applications or mobile apps.

questions.prompt: Which of the following scenarios best demonstrates a limitation of relying solely on Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)?

options.text: A user needs permission to edit only their own profile documents, but the 'Editor' role grants access to all documents.
An administrator needs to be assigned multiple roles simultaneously.
The system has too many users assigned to the 'Viewer' role.
A newly hired employee needs to be provisioned with standard organizational permissions.

questions.explanation: RBAC assigns permissions to roles rather than individual resources or context. When access depends on ownership (e.g., 'edit only my own profile'), Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) or fine-grained policies are typically required.

questions.prompt: An application uses JWTs stored in local storage for authentication. What is the primary security vulnerability introduced by this implementation choice?

options.text: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) via automatic cookie transmission.
SQL Injection vulnerabilities in the token decoding pipeline.
Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) allowing malicious scripts to read the token from storage.
Man-in-the-middle decryption of the JWT payload without a TLS certificate.

questions.explanation: Local storage is accessible by any JavaScript running on the page. If the application suffers from an XSS vulnerability, malicious scripts can exfiltrate the JWT from local storage.

questions.prompt: When implementing token revocation for stateless JWTs, which architectural pattern is commonly used to handle tokens that need to be invalidated before their natural expiration time?

options.text: Broadcasting a revocation event via WebSockets to all active browsers.
Checking a server-side blacklist or token revocation cache on each authenticated request.
Modifying the cryptographic secret key globally to invalidate all issued tokens instantly.
Compressing the JWT payload so the server can reject it based on size.

questions.explanation: Because JWTs are inherently stateless, checking a fast, server-side store (like Redis) for blacklisted token IDs (jti) or user session versions allows for immediate revocation.
